subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Capital expenditure is spending on:
questions.explain: Capital expenditure buys long-term assets (e.g. machinery); revenue expenditure covers day-to-day costs.

questions.q: Retained profit is an example of:
questions.explain: Retained profit and sale of assets are internal sources; loans and share capital are external.

questions.q: A bank overdraft is best suited to:
questions.explain: Overdrafts are flexible short-term finance; long-term assets need long-term finance.

questions.q: Issuing shares raises:
questions.explain: Selling shares raises equity finance from shareholders.

questions.q: A start-up with no trading history raises small amounts from many online backers. This is:
questions.explain: Crowdfunding raises funds from many people, often online, suited to start-ups.

questions.q: Fixed costs are costs that:
options: Do not change with the level of output
questions.explain: Fixed costs (e.g. rent) stay the same regardless of output; variable costs change with output.

questions.q: Contribution per unit equals selling price per unit minus:
questions.explain: Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit; it contributes to covering fixed costs.

questions.q: Total revenue is calculated as price multiplied by:
questions.explain: Total revenue = price × quantity sold.

questions.q: The statement of financial position (balance sheet) shows:
options: Assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time
questions.explain: The balance sheet is a snapshot of what a firm owns and owes at a moment.

questions.q: Net profit (profit for the period) is gross profit minus:
questions.explain: Gross profit − expenses = net profit (profit for the period).

questions.q: Gross profit margin is calculated as (gross profit ÷ sales revenue) ×:
questions.explain: Gross profit margin (%) = gross profit / sales revenue × 100.

questions.q: The current ratio is a measure of:
questions.explain: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities, indicating short-term liquidity.

questions.q: A current ratio of 0.5:1 suggests the firm:
options: May struggle to pay its short-term liabilities
questions.explain: Below 1:1 means current assets are less than current liabilities — a liquidity concern.

questions.q: Cash flow differs from profit because:
options: Profit can include credit sales and non-cash items; cash flow is actual money in and out
questions.explain: A profitable firm can still run out of cash (e.g. slow-paying customers).

questions.q: Working capital equals current assets minus:
questions.explain: Working capital = current assets − current liabilities, funding day-to-day operations.

questions.q: The payback period is:
options: The time taken to recover the initial investment
The total profit of a project
questions.explain: Payback measures how long cash inflows take to repay the initial outlay.

questions.q: Net present value (NPV) works by discounting future cash flows to:
questions.explain: NPV discounts future cash flows to today's value using a discount rate, then subtracts the initial cost.

questions.q: If an investment project has a positive NPV, it is generally:
questions.explain: A positive NPV means discounted returns exceed the cost, so the project adds value.

questions.q: Leasing an asset instead of buying it means the firm:
options: Pays to use it without owning it, lowering upfront cost
Owns it immediately with no payments
questions.explain: Leasing spreads cost over time and avoids a large upfront outlay, though total cost may be higher.

questions.q: A gross profit margin that rises year on year generally suggests:
questions.explain: A higher gross profit margin means more gross profit is kept from each unit of sales.

specSource: IB Diploma Business Management guide (first assessment 2024); Unit 3 — Finance and accounts
